accuracy.evidence: The two curriculum statements were checked against the DfE 2013 English programmes of study: Year 1 reading comprehension 'linking what they read or hear read to their own experiences' and Year 2 'drawing on what they already know or on background information and vocabulary'. Text-to-self and text-to-world connection terms follow Keene and Zimmermann (Mosaic of Thought). The world-knowledge facts in step 4 and the challenge (seeds need water, snow and chocolate melt in heat, rain makes you wet) and the word meanings in step 5 (soaked, exhausted, delicious, shivered, famished, stomped) were checked against the Oxford Learner's Dictionary.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the documented weak-connection habits named in the adult text: surface links on a shared name (step 1 'name' cards, challenge 'name'), surface links on a shared word or object (step 1 'word' cards: 'I went to a shop for milk' for a lost-in-a-shop story; challenge 'word', 'surface'), projecting one's own feeling onto a character against the text (step 3 clue words smiles, laughs, cries, hides; challenge 'self'), and predicting from a wish rather than world knowledge (step 4 wrong guesses, challenge 'life').

lab_distinct.evidence: flagremind is built around a story page that the learner links to their own memories: memory cards dropped on the book, a feeling borrowed from 'a time you lost a toy' dropped onto a face, a clue-word tap that overrules the feeling most people would have, and a new word worked out from a remembered experience. flaglink (Connecting New & Old Ideas) links a new science idea to a known analogy and tests where it breaks; flaginfer and flagclue work on inference from the text alone with no personal memory. The lab_distinct gate passed under 30% against every flagship lab.

lab_teaches.evidence: The child finds out by trying: dropping 'My friend is called Maya' on the book returns 'Same name, but that is all. It does not help you get the story', while the real memory returns 'This reminds me: My tooth was wobbly too.' In step 3 they read 'Lots of people feel scared here' and then tap smiles, which confirms 'they feel happy, not scared'. Each done screen sums up the rule (A good link: the same thing happened to me; the story wins).

predictions.evidence: Three predictions each offer a tempting wrong answer that the lab then disproves: that a same-name memory helps with Maya's wobbly tooth (step 1 rejects it), that Leo must be scared at the dentist because I would be (step 3 shows he smiles), and that Sid laughed in the snow (step 5 shows shivered means shook with cold).

challenge_feedback.evidence: Six challenge questions; each wrong option has its own message: 'name' (same name, nothing the same happened), 'word' (shares fish, but not a pet dying), 'feel' (think of falling and getting hurt), 'self' (you love the dark but Bea says she hates it, the story's words win), 'life' (the hot sun melts ice), 'word2' (stomping is loud and heavy, tiptoe is soft), 'surface' (liking the cover is not about what happens) and 'off'.

readability.evidence: Kid paragraphs use short, concrete sentences ('Think how you felt. Then you can guess how the boy in the book feels.'); the kid grade measured 0.2 against the family limit of 5.0 and the adult text 8.6 against 10.0. Story lines in the lab are one or two short sentences, and the step 1 banner was shortened to 'Story 1 of 5: which memory fits?' after the 360 px screenshot showed the longer text shrinking.

no_filler.evidence: Every kid sentence gives an action or an example (say it out loud, the same thing or the same feeling, read the words too); the adult paragraphs give the curriculum statements, what makes a link useful, the named mistakes and what each lab step does. The content gate found no filler phrases, and the explanation is under 12% the same as any other lesson, including Connecting New & Old Ideas and Inferring Characters' Feelings.

mobile.evidence: Checked on 360 px wide screenshots in light and dark themes for every step, before and after Show me: the story page, memory cards (54 px tall) and feeling tiles fit; the step 5 meanings were moved from a three-card column, which clipped the last card at 360 px, to a row of three 56 px tiles, and the hint now wraps above them without overlap. The walkthrough passed on iPhone 13.

accessibility.evidence: Every drag has a matching button below the canvas (memory buttons 'Link the story to: ...', feeling buttons, one button per word of the story line for the clue tap, guess and meaning buttons), and a plain tap on a card also counts as choosing it. The canvas aria-label is updated with every feedback message, the challenge feedback is a role=status live region, and axe (WCAG 2.1 AA) found no violations in either theme on desktop and iPhone 13.

sources: Department for Education (2013) The national curriculum in England: English programmes of study, Year 1 and Year 2 reading comprehension
Keene, E. O. and Zimmermann, S. (1997) Mosaic of Thought: text-to-self, text-to-text and text-to-world connections
Education Endowment Foundation (2020) Improving Literacy in Key Stage 1: activating prior knowledge and building vocabulary
